title: Binary Search
problem: Given a sorted (ascending) array of distinct integers nums and a target, return the index of target, or -1 if it is not present. You must write an O(log n) algorithm.
intuition: Because the array is sorted, comparing target with the middle element tells you which half the target must be in. If nums[mid] < target, everything at or left of mid is too small, so discard it. If nums[mid] > target, discard mid and everything to its right. Each step halves the search space, so you need about log2(n) steps.
Trace on the example: lo=0, hi=5, mid=2 (3 < 9, lo=3); mid=4 (9 == 9) → return 4.
notes: Say it like this: "A linear scan is O(n). Since the array is sorted, I compare with the middle and discard half each time, giving O(log n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: single element; target smaller than all or larger than all; empty array (loop never runs).
Common mistakes: while (lo < hi) with hi = n - 1 misses the last candidate; mid = (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow in Java for huge indices; forgetting +1 / -1 causes infinite loops.

Follow-ups: "Find first/last occurrence with duplicates?" Keep searching after a match: record ans = mid and move hi = mid - 1 (first) or lo = mid + 1 (last). "Lower bound / insert position?" Return lo when the loop ends. 4.2
simple: Find a number's position in a sorted list, or say it isn't there.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Scan every index from left to right.
Return the index where nums[i] == target, else -1.
approaches.why: We may look at every element once and use no extra storage.
approaches.simple: Look at every position from left to right until you find it.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary Search)
steps: Set lo = 0, hi = n - 1.
While lo <= hi, compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 (avoids overflow of lo + hi).
If nums[mid] == target return mid; if smaller, lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1.
If the loop ends, return -1.
approaches.why: The search range halves every iteration; only a few integer variables are used.
approaches.simple: Look at the middle. If the target is bigger, throw away the left half; if smaller, throw away the right half. Repeat, halving the search every time.

title: Find Minimum In Rotated Sorted Array
problem: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated some number of times (for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] became [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Return the minimum element in O(log n) time.
example: Explanation: The original array was [1,2,3,4,5], rotated 3 times.
intuition: A rotated sorted array is two sorted runs: a "high" run followed by a "low" run. The minimum is the first element of the low run. Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]: - If nums[mid] > nums[hi], then mid is in the high run and the drop (the minimum) is strictly to the right of mid. - Otherwise nums[mid] <= nums[hi], so mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left.
Why compare with nums[hi] and not nums[lo]? If the array is not rotated at all, nums[mid] > nums[lo] would wrongly push us right. Comparing with hi works in every case.
notes: Say it like this: "A linear scan is O(n). The array is two sorted halves, and comparing mid with the last element tells me which half mid is in, so I can discard half each time: O(log n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: not rotated at all ([1,2,3]); one element; two elements ([2,1]).
Common mistakes: using hi = mid - 1 when nums[mid] <= nums[hi] (skips the answer); using while (lo <= hi) with hi = mid (infinite loop).

Follow-ups: "How many times was it rotated?" It is the index of the minimum. "What if duplicates are allowed (LC 154)?" When nums[mid] == nums[hi] you cannot decide, so do hi--; worst case becomes O(n). 4.3
simple: A sorted list was rotated (cut and its two pieces swapped). Find the smallest number.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Scan the whole array and track the minimum.
approaches.why: One pass over all elements, constant extra variables.
approaches.simple: Scan everything and keep the smallest.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary Search against the right end)
steps: lo = 0, hi = n - 1.
While lo < hi: mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the minimum is right of mid: lo = mid + 1.
Else the minimum is at mid or left: hi = mid (do not skip mid, it may be the answer).
When lo == hi, that index holds the minimum.
approaches.why: Every step halves the range; no extra storage.
approaches.simple: Compare the middle with the last number. If the middle is bigger, the drop (and the minimum) is to the right; otherwise it is at mid or to the left.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
problem: There are n piles of bananas, piles[i] in pile i. Koko picks an eating speed k bananas/hour. Each hour she picks one pile and eats k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer, she finishes it and waits for the rest of that hour). Find the minimum integer k that lets her finish all piles within h hours. It is guaranteed that h >= n.
example: Explanation: At k=4 hours needed = 1+2+2+3 = 8 <= 8. At k=3 it is 1+2+3+4 = 10 > 8.
intuition: We are not searching inside piles; we are searching for the speed k. The key observation: if Koko can finish at speed k, she can finish at any speed bigger than k. So "feasible(k)" looks like F F F T T T over k = 1, 2, 3,... and we want the first T. That monotonic yes/no is exactly what binary search on the answer needs.

The answer lies in [1, max(piles)]: at speed max(piles) each pile takes exactly one hour, so total hours is n <= h, and a faster speed never helps. Hours for a pile at speed k is ceil(p / k), computed with integers as (p + k - 1) / k.
notes: Say it like this: "Trying every speed from 1 to max is O(n·max). Feasibility is monotonic in speed, so I binary search the speed in [1, max] and check each candidate in O(n), for O(n log max) overall and O(1) space."
Edge cases: h == n (answer is max(piles)); one pile; very large piles (up to 10^9).

Common mistakes: summing hours in int (overflows when k is small and piles are large); (p + k - 1) can overflow if p is near Integer.MAX_VALUE, use (p - 1) / k + 1 or long if so; starting lo at 0 (division by zero).

Follow-ups: "What is the general pattern?" Minimize a value subject to a monotonic feasibility check: Ship Packages Within D Days, Minimum Days to Make Bouquets, Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold all use the same template. 4.4
simple: Koko eats bananas at k per hour, one pile at a time. Find the slowest speed that finishes within h hours.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Try every speed k from 1 to max(piles).
For each, compute total hours; return the first k with hours <= h.
approaches.why: Up to max speeds, each needs a full pass over n piles.
approaches.simple: Try speed 1, 2, 3, … and return the first one that finishes in time.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary Search on speed)
steps: lo = 1, hi = max(piles), ans = hi.
While lo <= hi: mid is a candidate speed; compute total hours.
If hours <= h, mid works: record ans = mid, try slower (hi = mid - 1).
Else it is too slow: lo = mid + 1.
Return ans.
approaches.why: log(max) binary search steps, each a linear pass to compute hours.
approaches.simple: Faster speeds always finish sooner, so binary search the speed: if mid works, try slower; if not, go faster.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problem: Given two sorted arrays nums1 (size m) and nums2 (size n), return the median of the combined sorted array. The required run time is O(log(m + n)).
example: Explanation: Merged array is [1,2,3]; the median is 2.
intuition: The median splits the merged array into a left half and a right half of equal size (left gets the extra element when the total is odd), with every left element <= every right element. We never need to build the merged array: we only need to decide how many elements of the left half come from nums1. Call that cut1; then cut2 = half - cut1 come from nums2, where half = (m + n + 1) / 2.

A split is correct when the last left element of each array is <= the first right element of the other: L1 <= R2 and L2 <= R1. If L1 > R2, we took too many from nums1, so move cut1 left. If L2 > R1, we took too few, so move cut1 right. That decision is monotonic in cut1, so binary search on cut1 over the smaller array gives O(log(min(m, n))).

Use -infinity for "nothing on the left" and +infinity for "nothing on the right" so the boundary cases need no special code. Trace [1,3], [2]: search on nums2 (smaller), m'=1, n'=2, half=2. lo=0, hi=1, cut1=0 (from [2]), cut2=2: L1=-inf, R1=2, L2=3, R2=+inf. L2 > R1 → lo=1. cut1=1, cut2=1: L1=2, R1=+inf, L2=1, R2=3. Valid; odd total → max(L1, L2) = 2.
notes: Say it like this: "Merging is O(m+n) time and space, and I can cut space to O(1) by only counting to the middle. For O(log) I binary search how many elements of the smaller array go into the left half; the rest come from the other array, and I check the cross conditions L1 <= R2 and L2 <= R1. That is O(log(min(m,n))) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: one array empty; all of nums1 smaller than nums2 (cut1 = m); even total; negative numbers; duplicates across arrays.

Common mistakes: binary searching the larger array (cut2 can go negative); integer division when averaging ((a + b) / 2 in Java truncates, and a + b can overflow, so cast to double first); wrong half for odd totals.
Follow-ups: "Find the k-th smallest of two sorted arrays?" Same partition idea with half = k (see 4.17). "Why min(m, n)?" Searching the smaller array guarantees cut2 stays in [0, n]. 4.5
simple: Find the median of two sorted lists put together.

approaches.label: Brute Force (merge everything)
steps: Merge both arrays into one sorted array of size m + n with two pointers.
If the size is odd, return the middle element; else the average of the two middle ones.
approaches.why: The merge visits every element once and stores all of them.
approaches.simple: Merge both lists into one sorted list and pick the middle.

approaches.label: Better (merge only until the middle)
steps: Walk the two pointers as in a merge, but do not store anything.
Remember only the elements at merged positions total/2 - 1 and total/2.
Stop once position total/2 is reached and compute the median from those two.
approaches.why: We still walk about half of the elements, but only keep two values.
approaches.simple: Merge only in your head, step by step, and stop once you reach the middle.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on the partition)
steps: Make nums1 the smaller array (swap if needed). Let half = (m + n + 1) / 2.
Binary search cut1 in [0, m]; set cut2 = half - cut1.
L1 = nums1[cut1-1] (or -inf), R1 = nums1[cut1] (or +inf), same for L2, R2 on nums2.
If L1 <= R2 && L2 <= R1: found. Odd total → max(L1, L2); even → (max(L1, L2) + min(R1, R2)) / 2.
Else if L1 > R2: hi = cut1 - 1. Else: lo = cut1 + 1.
approaches.why: We binary search only over the cut positions of the smaller array, using a few variables.
approaches.simple: Binary search where to cut the smaller list so that the left parts of both lists together hold exactly half of the numbers and every left number is ≤ every right number.

title: Search In Rotated Sorted Array
problem: A sorted array of distinct integers has been rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the rotated array nums and a target, return the index of target or -1. Required time is O(log n).
intuition: Cut a rotated array anywhere and at least one side of mid is fully sorted. Find out which side: if nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left part lo..mid is sorted; otherwise the right part mid..hi is sorted. On the sorted side you can check with a simple range test whether the target lies there. If yes, search that side; if no, it must be on the other side.
Trace: lo=0, hi=6, mid=3 (7). Left [4..7] is sorted; 0 is not in [4,7] → lo=4. lo=4, hi=6, mid=5 (1). Left [0..1] sorted; 0 in [0,1) → hi=4. mid=4 → found.
notes: Say it like this: "Linear scan is O(n). In a rotated sorted array one side of mid is always sorted; I identify it, check if the target falls in its range, and discard the other half. That is O(log n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: array not rotated; one or two elements; target equals nums[lo] or nums[hi].
Common mistakes: nums[lo] < nums[mid] instead of <= (breaks when lo == mid, e.g. two elements); wrong strict/non-strict bounds in the range check.
Follow-ups: "With duplicates?" See 4.9: when nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], shrink both ends; worst case O(n). 4.6
simple: Search for a target in a sorted list that has been rotated.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Linear scan for the target.
approaches.why: Checks each element once, no extra memory.
approaches.simple: Scan for it.

approaches.label: Better (find the pivot, then two normal binary searches)
steps: Find the index of the minimum (pivot) with the method from 4.2.
The array is sorted on [0, pivot-1] and on [pivot, n-1]. Run a standard binary search on whichever range could contain the target.
approaches.why: Two binary searches of O(log n) each. Same complexity as optimal but two passes; it is still a perfectly good answer and easier to get right under pressure.
approaches.simple: First find where the rotation happened, then do normal binary search in the correct sorted piece.

approaches.label: Optimal (one-pass binary search)
steps: lo = 0, hi = n - 1. While lo <= hi, compute mid; return it if it is the target.
If nums[lo] <= nums[mid] (left half sorted): if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid] go left (hi = mid - 1), else go right.
Else (right half sorted): if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi] go right (lo = mid + 1), else go left.
Return -1 if not found.
approaches.why: Each iteration discards half of the range; constant variables.
approaches.simple: One binary search: at each step one half is always properly sorted. Check if the target fits inside that sorted half; if not, it must be in the other half.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
problem: You get an m x n matrix where each row is sorted left to right, and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. Return true if target is in the matrix. Required time is O(log(m · n)).
intuition: Because each row continues where the previous one stopped, reading the matrix row by row gives one fully sorted array of length m · n. You do not have to build it: index k of that virtual array is matrix[k / n][k % n]. Then it is just Binary Search (4.1).
notes: Say it like this: "Scanning is O(mn). Because rows chain into one sorted sequence, I binary search a virtual 1D array and map index k to (k / n, k % n). O(log(mn)) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: single row or single column; target smaller than matrix[0][0] or larger than the last cell.
Common mistakes: dividing by m instead of n (columns) in the mapping; m * n overflowing for giant matrices (not an issue under LeetCode limits).
Follow-ups: "What if only rows and columns are sorted separately?" That is 4.11: start from the top-right corner, O(m + n). 4.7
simple: Search a matrix where each row is sorted and each row starts after the previous row ends.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Check every cell.
approaches.why: Every cell is visited once.
approaches.simple: Check every cell.

approaches.label: Better (pick the row, then binary search in it)
steps: For each row, if row[0] <= target <= row[n-1], the target can only be in this row.
Binary search that one row.
approaches.why: Linear walk down the first column, then one binary search on a row. (Binary searching the row too would make it O(log m + log n), which equals the optimal.)
approaches.simple: Find the one row whose range can contain the target, then binary search that row.

approaches.label: Optimal (treat as one sorted array)
steps: lo = 0, hi = m · n - 1.
mid maps to matrix[mid / n][mid % n]. Compare with target and halve as usual.
approaches.why: One binary search over m · n virtual positions.
approaches.simple: Read the matrix as one long sorted list and binary search it, turning a position into (row, column).

title: Time Based Key Value Store
problem: Design TimeMap: set(key, value, timestamp) stores a value for a key at a time; get(key, timestamp) returns the value set for key with the largest timestamp <= timestamp, or "" if none. Timestamps passed to set are strictly increasing.
example: Explanation: get("foo",3) has no entry at 3, so the latest at or before 3 is "bar" at 1.
intuition: Group entries by key in a hash map. Because set timestamps arrive in increasing order, each key's list is already sorted by timestamp just by appending. A get is then "find the last timestamp <= t ", a classic upper-bound binary search on that list.
notes: Say it like this: "I store, per key, a list of (timestamp, value). Since set timestamps are increasing, the list is sorted for free. A backward scan makes get O(k); binary searching for the last timestamp <= t makes get O(log k), with set O(1)."
Edge cases: key never set; query timestamp earlier than the first set for that key; many keys with one entry each.
Common mistakes: sorting on every set (unnecessary, timestamps are increasing); returning null instead of ""; using < instead of <=.

Follow-ups: "What if timestamps are not increasing?" Use a TreeMap<Integer, String> per key and call floorEntry(t): O(log k) for both set and get. In Java that is also a neat one-line alternative to the manual binary search. 4.8
simple: Store values with timestamps and answer "what was the value at time t?" using the latest value at or before t.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Map each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs, appended in order.
On get, scan the list from the end backwards and return the first value with timestamp <= t.
approaches.time: set O(1), get O(k) where k is the number of entries for that key
approaches.why: Linear scan of one key's history per get; every set is stored once.
approaches.simple: Keep each key's history in a list and scan backwards for the right time.

approaches.label: Optimal (binary search per key)
steps: Same storage: key → list of pairs in increasing timestamp order.
On get, binary search for the rightmost index with time <= t: if time[mid] <= t, record it and go right; else go left.
Return the recorded value, or "".
approaches.time: set O(1) amortized, get O(log k)
approaches.why: Appending to an array list is amortized O(1); each get is a binary search over one key's entries.
approaches.simple: Timestamps are added in order, so the history is sorted; binary search for the last time ≤ t.

title: Find Peak Element
problem: A peak element is strictly greater than its neighbours. Given nums where nums[i]!= nums[i+1], return the index of any peak. Imagine nums[-1] = nums[n] = -infinity. Required time is O(log n).
example: Explanation: 6 at index 5 is a peak (index 1, value 2, is also valid).
intuition: Look at the slope at mid. If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], you are walking uphill to the right. Since the array ends with -infinity, the climb must come down at some point, so a peak must exist to the right of mid. Otherwise (nums[mid] > nums[mid+1]) you are going downhill, and mid itself or something to its left is a peak (because nums[-1] = -infinity). Either way you can throw away half.
The array is not sorted, but binary search still works because we always keep a half that is guaranteed to contain an answer.
notes: Say it like this: "Checking every index is O(n). If mid is on an upward slope, a peak must lie to the right because the right end is minus infinity; otherwise there is one at mid or to the left. So I binary search on the slope in O(log n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: single element (it is a peak); strictly increasing (last index); strictly decreasing (index 0).
Common mistakes: thinking binary search needs a sorted array; using lo <= hi and then reading nums[mid + 1] out of bounds.
Follow-ups: "Which peak does it return?" Any one, not necessarily the global maximum (finding the global max needs O(n)). "2D version?" See 4.12. 4.9
simple: Find any element bigger than its neighbours.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each index, check it is greater than both neighbours (treating out-of-range as -infinity).
Return the first such index.
approaches.why: Each index is checked once against two neighbours.
approaches.simple: Check every position against its neighbours.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on the slope)
steps: lo = 0, hi = n - 1. While lo < hi:
mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 (so mid + 1 <= hi is always valid).
If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]: peak is to the right, lo = mid + 1.
Else: peak is at mid or to the left, hi = mid.
Return lo.
approaches.why: Halves the range every step, constant extra space.
approaches.simple: If the next number is bigger, you are walking uphill, so a peak must exist to the right. Otherwise a peak is here or to the left. Binary search on that slope.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
pattern: Binary search on rotated array with duplicates
problem: Same as 4.5, but the array may contain duplicates. Return true if target is present, else false.
intuition: The 4.5 trick needs to know which half is sorted. With duplicates, the case nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] (for example [1,0,1,1,1]) tells you nothing: the dip could be on either side. But in that case nums[lo] and nums[hi] are equal to nums[mid], which we already know is not the target, so we can safely drop both ends: lo++, hi--. In every other case, the 4.5 logic works unchanged.
notes: Say it like this: "Linear scan is O(n). I reuse the rotated-array search; the only new case is when lo, mid and hi are all equal, where I cannot tell which half is sorted, so I shrink both ends. Average O(log n), worst O(n), O(1) space."
Edge cases: all elements equal; target equal to the repeated value; [1,0,1,1,1] with target 0.
Common mistakes: shrinking only when nums[lo] == nums[mid] without also checking nums[hi] (works but is less clear); claiming the worst case is still O(log n).
Follow-ups: "Can you beat O(n) worst case?" No: with [1,1,1,...,0,...,1] any algorithm may need to inspect every element to find the 0. 4.10
simple: Search a rotated sorted list that can contain duplicates.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Linear scan.
approaches.why: Each element checked once.
approaches.simple: Scan for it.

approaches.label: Optimal (binary search, shrink on ambiguity)
steps: Standard lo <= hi loop; return true if nums[mid] == target.
If nums[lo] == nums[mid] && nums[mid] == nums[hi]: lo++, hi--, continue.
Else apply the 4.5 rule: find the sorted half and check if target is in its range.
approaches.time: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case
approaches.why: When many equal values force the shrink step, we only remove two elements per step (e.g. all elements equal except one).
approaches.simple: Same as rotated search, but when the left, middle and right values are equal you can't tell which half is sorted, so just shrink both ends by one.

title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
problem: A sorted array contains every element exactly twice except one element that appears once. Find that single element in O(log n) time and O(1) space.
example: Explanation: Every other value appears twice.
intuition: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices: (0,1), (2,3),.... After the single element, everything shifts by one, so pairs start at odd indices. So at any even index i, if nums[i] == nums[i+1] the single element is to the right; if not, it is at i or to the left. To always look at an even index, make mid even (if mid is odd, do mid- -).
Trace: lo=0, hi=8. mid=4 (even): nums[4]=3, nums[5]=4, not equal → hi=4. mid=2: nums[2]=2, nums[3]=3, not equal → hi=2. mid=1 → make even, mid=0: nums[0]==nums[1] → lo=2. lo == hi = 2 → answer 2.
notes: Say it like this: "XOR gives O(n). Using sortedness: before the single element pairs start at even indices, after it at odd ones. I binary search on even indices and check whether the pair is intact, in O(log n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: single element array; answer at index 0; answer at the last index.

Common mistakes: not forcing mid to be even; lo = mid + 1 instead of mid + 2 (breaks parity); reading nums[mid + 1] out of bounds (cannot happen while lo < hi and mid is even, since hi is always even).
Follow-ups: "Alternative without the even trick?" Use mid ^ 1 as the partner index: compare nums[mid] with nums[mid ^ 1]; equal means go right. 4.11
simple: Every number appears twice except one. The list is sorted. Find the single one.

approaches.label: Brute Force (XOR)
steps: XOR all elements. Equal pairs cancel out (a ^ a = 0), leaving the single element.
approaches.why: One pass. Note this works even when the array is not sorted, but ignores the sortedness.
approaches.simple: XOR all numbers; pairs cancel and the single one is left.

approaches.label: Optimal (binary search on even indices)
steps: lo = 0, hi = n - 1. While lo < hi:
mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if mid is odd, mid--.
If nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1]: the pair is intact, single is after it: lo = mid + 2.
Else: single is at mid or before: hi = mid.
Return nums[lo].
approaches.why: Range halves every step; constant variables.
approaches.simple: Before the single number, pairs start at even positions; after it, pairs start at odd positions. Binary search for where that pattern breaks.

title: Search a 2D Matrix II
problem: In an m x n matrix, each row is sorted ascending left to right and each column is sorted ascending top to bottom (rows do not continue each other). Return true if target is present.
intuition: Stand at the top-right corner. Every value to its left is smaller, every value below is bigger. So the corner works like the root of a binary search tree: - value > target: the whole column below is even bigger, so drop this column (move left). - value < target: the whole row to the left is even smaller, so drop this row (move down).
Each step removes a full row or column, so at most m + n steps. The bottom-left corner works symmetrically. Top-left and bottom-right do not work, because both directions go the same way.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force is O(mn), and binary searching every row is O(m log n). From the top-right corner, each comparison removes a whole row or column, so the staircase walk is O(m + n) with O(1) space."
Edge cases: 1 x 1 matrix; target smaller than matrix[0][0] or larger than matrix[m-1][n-1].
Common mistakes: starting at top-left (both moves increase, no decision possible); trying the flatten trick from 4.6 (invalid here because rows do not chain).
Follow-ups: "When is m log n better than m + n?" When one dimension is much smaller: if m is tiny and n is huge, binary search on rows (or on the shorter dimension) wins: O(min · log max). 4.12
simple: Search a matrix where every row and every column is sorted.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Check every cell.
approaches.why: Visits every cell once.
approaches.simple: Check every cell.

approaches.label: Better (binary search each row)
steps: For every row, binary search for the target (skip rows whose range cannot contain it).
approaches.why: One O(log n) search per row.
approaches.simple: Binary search inside each row.

approaches.label: Optimal (staircase from top-right)
steps: Start at r = 0, c = n - 1.
While inside the matrix: if equal, return true; if greater than target, c--; else r++.
Return false when you walk out.
approaches.why: Each step eliminates one row or one column, so at most m + n steps.
approaches.simple: Start at the top-right corner. Too big? Move left. Too small? Move down. Each step rules out a whole row or column.

title: Find a Peak Element II
problem: In an m x n grid where no two adjacent cells are equal, a peak is a cell strictly greater than its up, down, left and right neighbours (the grid is surrounded by -1). Return the [row, col] of any peak in O(m log n) or O(n log m) time.
example: Explanation: 30 is greater than 20, 21, 14 and 16. ([2,2] with 32 is also valid.)
intuition: Binary search on columns. For the middle column, find the row of its maximum value. That cell is already bigger than its up and down neighbours (it is the column max). Now compare it with its left and right neighbours: - Bigger than both → it is a peak. - Left neighbour is bigger → go left. Why is a peak guaranteed there? Climbing from a larger value leftwards, the column-max of whatever column we land on is at least that big, so we can never be forced back across. Same logic as 1D peak (4.8), with "column max" playing the role of a single value. - Otherwise right neighbour is bigger → go right.
notes: Say it like this: "Checking every cell, or taking the global maximum, is O(mn). I binary search over columns: the max of the middle column beats its vertical neighbours, and if a horizontal neighbour is bigger I move toward it, just like 1D peak finding. O(m log n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: single column (column max is the answer); single row (reduces to 4.8); peak on the border.
Common mistakes: taking any cell of the middle column instead of the column maximum (then up/down neighbours are not guaranteed smaller); forgetting the -1 boundary.
Follow-ups: "If m is much larger than n?" Binary search on rows instead and scan each middle row for its max: O(n log m). Pick the smaller dimension to scan. 4.13
simple: In a grid, find a cell larger than all four neighbours.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Check every cell against its four neighbours.
approaches.why: Every cell, constant work each.
approaches.simple: Check every cell against its neighbours.

approaches.label: Better (global maximum)
steps: The largest value in the whole grid is always a peak (nothing around it can be bigger). Find it in one pass.
approaches.why: Same complexity as brute force but simpler and a good thing to mention; it does not meet the required bound.
approaches.simple: The biggest number in the whole grid is automatically a peak.

approaches.label: Optimal (binary search on columns)
steps: lo = 0, hi = n - 1. While lo <= hi: mid column.
Find row = index of the max in column mid (O(m)).
left = mid > 0? mat[row][mid-1]: -1, right = mid < n-1? mat[row][mid+1]: -1.
If mat[row][mid] > left && mat[row][mid] > right return [row, mid].
Else if left > mat[row][mid]: hi = mid - 1; else lo = mid + 1.
approaches.why: log n column choices, each needing an O(m) scan for the column max.
approaches.simple: Binary search on columns: take the biggest cell in the middle column, then move toward a bigger neighbour on the left or right.

title: Find Nth Root of a Number
problem: Given two positive integers n and m, find the integer x such that x^n == m. If no integer satisfies it, return -1. (GFG / Striver problem; on GFG the method is NthRoot(n, m).)
example: Explanation: 3^3 = 27. For n = 4, m = 69 the answer is -1 because 2^4 = 16 and 3^4 = 81.
intuition: x^n grows as x grows, so the function is monotonic in x. The answer, if it exists, lies in [1, m]. Binary search on x: if mid^n is too small go right, if too big go left.

The trap is overflow: mid^n for mid around 10^9 and n = 3 blows past long. Fix: multiply step by step and stop as soon as the product exceeds m. Return a three-way result (less / equal / greater) instead of the actual power.
notes: Say it like this: "Trying each x is slow for small n. Since x^n is increasing in x, I binary search x in [1, m] and compare mid^n with m using an early-exit multiply to avoid overflow. O(n log m) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: m = 1 (answer 1 for any n); n = 1 (answer m); perfect power vs not.
Common mistakes: using Math.pow (floating point error for large values, e.g. Math.pow(x, n) returning 26.999...); computing the full power and overflowing long.

Follow-ups: "Real-valued root to 6 decimals?" Binary search on doubles for a fixed number of iterations (e.g. 100) or until hi - lo < 1e-7. "Integer square root (LC 69)?" Same template, return hi (the floor) when not exact. 4.14
simple: Find a whole number x so that x to the power n equals m, or −1 if none exists.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Try x = 1, 2, 3,...; compute x^n with early exit.
If it equals m return x; once it exceeds m, stop and return -1.
approaches.why: We try up to the root of m values (we stop once the power overshoots), each power costing up to n multiplications. For n = 1 this degrades to O(m).
approaches.simple: Try x = 1, 2, 3, … until x^n reaches or passes m.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on x)
steps: lo = 1, hi = m.
For mid, compute cmp(mid): multiply mid n times, returning 2 (greater) as soon as the product exceeds m; at the end return 1 if equal, 0 if smaller.
Equal → return mid; smaller → lo = mid + 1; greater → hi = mid - 1.
Return -1.
approaches.why: log m binary search steps, each up to n multiplications.
approaches.simple: Binary search x between 1 and m, stopping the multiplication early once the product is already too big.

title: Aggressive Cows
pattern: Binary search on answer (maximize the minimum)
problem: You are given positions of n stalls (stalls, not necessarily sorted) and k cows. Place the cows in stalls so that the minimum distance between any two cows is as large as possible. Return that largest possible minimum distance. (GFG / Striver; 2 <= k <= n.)
example: Explanation: Place cows at 1, 4, 8 (gaps 3 and 4, minimum 3). No placement achieves minimum 4.
intuition: Turn the optimization into a yes/no question: "Can I place k cows so that every two are at least d apart?" Check it greedily on the sorted stalls: put the first cow in the first stall, then put each next cow in the first stall that is at least d away from the last placed cow. Greedy is safe because placing a cow as early as possible never leaves less room for the rest.
Monotonic: if distance d is achievable, every smaller distance is too. So feasibility looks like T T T T F F over d, and we want the last T. The answer is in [1, max - min].
Trace with d=4 on [1,2,4,8,9]: cow at 1, next stall >= 5 is 8, next >= 12 none → only 2 cows → not feasible. d=3: 1, 4, 8 → 3 cows → feasible. Answer 3.
notes: Say it like this: "I turn 'maximize the minimum distance' into 'can I place k cows with gap at least d', which a greedy left-to-right pass answers in O(n) after sorting. Feasibility is monotonic in d, so instead of trying every d I binary search it: O(n log n + n log(range)) time, O(1) extra space."
Edge cases: k == 2 (answer is max - min); k == n (answer is the smallest adjacent gap); unsorted input; duplicate stall positions (distance 0 between them).
Common mistakes: forgetting to sort; searching for the first feasible instead of the last (this is a maximize problem, so on success go right); starting hi at max instead of max - min.

Follow-ups: "Same pattern?" Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (LC 1552) is this exact problem. "Why is greedy placement optimal?" Exchange argument: any valid placement can shift its i-th cow left to the greedy's i-th stall without breaking the gaps. 4.15
simple: Place cows in stalls so the closest two cows are as far apart as possible.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Sort the stalls.
Try every distance d from 1 to max - min; run the greedy check.
The last feasible d is the answer (you can stop at the first infeasible one).
approaches.why: Each candidate distance costs one O(n) greedy pass.
approaches.simple: Sort the stalls and try every distance, checking greedily whether all cows fit.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on the distance)
steps: Sort the stalls. lo = 1, hi = max - min, ans = 0.
While lo <= hi: if canPlace(mid), record ans = mid and try bigger (lo = mid + 1); else hi = mid - 1.
Return ans.
approaches.time: O(n log n + n · log(max - min))
approaches.why: Sorting, then log(range) greedy checks of O(n) each.
approaches.simple: If a distance works, every smaller distance works too. Binary search the biggest distance that still fits all the cows.

title: Book Allocation Problem
pattern: Binary search on answer (minimize the maximum)
problem: arr[i] is the number of pages in book i. Allocate all books to k students so that each student gets at least one book, each book goes to exactly one student, and every student gets a contiguous block of books. Minimize the maximum number of pages assigned to any student. Return -1 if it is impossible (more students than books). (GFG findPages(arr, k).)
example: Explanation: Split [12,34,67] | [90] gives max(113, 90) = 113. Every other split has a bigger maximum.
intuition: Flip it into a yes/no question: "If no student may read more than limit pages, how many students do I need?" Answer greedily: give books to the current student until adding the next one would exceed limit, then start a new student. Fewer students needed as limit grows, so "students needed <= k" is monotonic: F F F T T T over limit. We want the first T.
Range: limit must be at least max(arr) (someone has to read the biggest book) and at most sum(arr) (one student reads everything).

Trace limit=113: 12+34+67 = 113 (student 1), 90 (student 2) → 2 students → feasible. limit=112: 12+34 = 46, then +67 = 113 > 112, so student 2 starts with 67, then +90 > 112, so student 3 → infeasible. Answer 113.
notes: Say it like this: "For a given page limit, a greedy pass tells me how many students I need, and that count only drops as the limit grows. So I binary search the limit between max(arr) and sum(arr) for the smallest one needing at most k students: O(n log(sum)) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: k > n → -1; k == n → answer is max(arr); k == 1 → answer is sum(arr); one huge book.

Common mistakes: starting lo at 0 or 1 instead of max(arr) (the greedy then breaks on a book bigger than the limit); checking == k instead of <= k (if fewer students suffice, you can always split further to use exactly k, since k <= n); sum overflow in int.
Follow-ups: "Same pattern?" Split Array Largest Sum (LC 410), Painter's Partition, Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (LC 1011) are the same problem with different stories. 4.16
simple: Give books (in order) to k students so the most pages any student reads is as small as possible.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: If k > n return -1.
Try every limit from max(arr) to sum(arr); return the first one where the greedy needs <= k students.
approaches.why: Each candidate limit costs one O(n) greedy pass.
approaches.simple: Try every page limit from the largest book upward until k students are enough.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on the page limit)
steps: If k > n return -1.
lo = max(arr), hi = sum(arr).
While lo <= hi: if studentsNeeded(mid) <= k, record ans = mid, try smaller (hi = mid - 1); else lo = mid + 1.
Return ans.
approaches.why: log(range) checks, each one greedy pass of O(n).
approaches.simple: Binary search the page limit; for each guess, count how many students you need by filling each student greedily.

title: Matrix Median
problem: Given an R x C matrix where every row is sorted and R · C is odd, return the median of all its elements. (GFG median(mat); the expected time is better than flattening and sorting.)
example: Explanation: Sorted elements: 1 2 3 3 5 6 6 9 9. The middle (5th of 9) is 5.
intuition: The median is the smallest value x such that more than half of the elements are <= x. With total = R · C and half = total / 2, the median is the smallest x with count(<= x) > half.

count(<= x) is monotonic in x, so binary search on the value x in [min of first column, max of last column]. Counting is fast because each row is sorted: an upper-bound binary search per row gives how many elements in that row are <= x.

Why is the found x actually in the matrix? Because it is the smallest value where the count jumps above half, and the count only changes at values that exist in the matrix. Trace: total = 9, half = 4. Range [1, 9]. mid=5: count(<=5) = 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 > 4 → ans=5, hi=4. mid=2: count = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 → lo=3. mid=3: count = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, not > 4 → lo=4. mid=4: count 4 → lo=5 > hi. Answer 5.
notes: Say it like this: "Flattening and sorting is O(RC log RC) time and O(RC) space. Instead I binary search the answer value: for a candidate x, I count elements <= x with an upper bound in each sorted row, and the median is the smallest x whose count exceeds half. O(R log C log(range)) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: single row or single column; negative numbers (use lo + (hi - lo) / 2, and in JS Math.floor rather than >> 1 for the value search); many duplicates.
Common mistakes: using count >= half instead of count > half (off by one, returns a smaller value); binary searching indices instead of values; assuming columns are sorted too.

Follow-ups: "Even number of elements?" Find the values with rank total/2 and total/2 + 1 the same way and average them. "Kth smallest in a row-and-column sorted matrix (LC 378)?" Same value-space binary search, count with the staircase walk from 4.11 in O(R + C). 4.17
simple: Find the median of a matrix whose rows are each sorted.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Copy all elements into one array and sort it.
Return the element at index total / 2.
approaches.why: Sorting all elements dominates; the copy holds all of them.
approaches.simple: Copy everything into one list, sort it, take the middle.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on value, count with upper bound)
steps: lo = min of mat[i][0], hi = max of mat[i][C-1]. half = (R · C) / 2.
While lo <= hi: count elements <= mid using an upper bound in every row.
If count > half, mid could be the median: ans = mid, hi = mid - 1. Else lo = mid + 1.
Return ans.
approaches.why: log(range) values tried; each count does R binary searches of log C.
approaches.simple: Binary search on the value: for a guess, count how many cells are ≤ it (binary search in each row). The first value where that count passes half is the median.

title: K-th Element of Two Sorted Arrays
problem: Given two sorted arrays a and b and an integer k (1-indexed), return the element that would be at position k if both arrays were merged into one sorted array. (GFG kthElement(a, b, k).)
intuition: Exactly the partition idea from Median of Two Sorted Arrays (4.4), but the left part has size k instead of half. Choose cut1 elements from a (the smaller array) and cut2 = k - cut1 from b. The split is valid when L1 <= R2 and L2 <= R1; then the k-th element is max(L1, L2).
The new detail is the range of cut1: it cannot be more than k or more than m, and it must be at least k - n (if b cannot supply enough elements, a must). So lo = max(0, k - n), hi = min(k, m).
notes: Say it like this: "Merging is O(m+n), and stopping after k steps is O(k) with O(1) space. For log time I binary search how many of the first k elements come from the smaller array, checking the cross conditions L1 <= R2 and L2 <= R1; the answer is max(L1, L2). O(log(min(m,n))) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: k = 1 (min of the two heads); k = m + n (max of the two tails); one array empty; k larger than the smaller array (lo = k - n matters when k exceeds the bigger array).
Common mistakes: lo = 0 and hi = m without clamping to k - n and k (cut2 goes negative or past n); treating k as 0-indexed.

Follow-ups: "How is the median a special case?" Median is the k-th element with k = (m + n + 1) / 2 (plus the next one for even totals). "Alternative O(log k) recursion?" Compare a[k/2 - 1] and b[k/2 - 1] and discard the smaller k/2 elements each round.
simple: Find the k-th smallest number across two sorted lists.

approaches.label: Brute Force (merge)
steps: Merge both arrays fully, return merged[k - 1].
approaches.why: Full merge of both arrays into a new one.
approaches.simple: Merge both lists and pick position k.

approaches.label: Better (two pointers, count to k)
steps: Walk the merge with two pointers, without storing, and stop after taking k elements.
The last element taken is the answer.
approaches.why: We take exactly k steps and keep only the latest value.
approaches.simple: Walk the merge with two fingers and stop after k steps.

approaches.label: Optimal (Binary search on the partition)
steps: Ensure a is the smaller array (swap otherwise). m = a.length, n = b.length.
lo = max(0, k - n), hi = min(k, m).
cut1 = mid, cut2 = k - cut1; compute L1, R1, L2, R2 with sentinels.
Valid (L1 <= R2 && L2 <= R1) → return max(L1, L2). If L1 > R2, hi = cut1 - 1; else lo = cut1 + 1.
approaches.why: Binary search over cut positions in the smaller array only.
approaches.simple: Binary search how many of the k numbers come from the first list; the rest come from the second. Check the cut is in the right order.
